newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azeri banking system seen heading for shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Azeri banking system seen heading for shake-up.

text.p: Azerbaijan's banking system is heading for a shake-up orchestrated by the government -- with a little help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, bankers said.
"We have some 120 banks at the moment and expect this number to be halved," Samir Sharifov, director of Forex at the National Bank of Azerbaijan, told Reuters.

Another leading banker made even more drastic forecasts, saying the number of survivors would probably drop to 40 or 50 and that the issuing of new licences for foreign banks had in practice been frozen.

On July 1, the minimum capital requirement for Azeri banks was increased to 600,000 dollars from 100,000 dollars a year ago. In the next 12 months, this requirement will be doubled, said the banking source, who asked not to be named.
"The small and under-capitalised banks are running out of steam. We will see either a wave of mergers or the withdrawal of licences," the source said.
Faced with a banking sector debt crisis, the government intervened in September 1996 and tied the hands of state-owned banks, barring them from accepting deposits or making loans.

The source said these regulations would be relaxed, but that a huge restructuring programme had been developed with the help of the World Bank and the IMF under which the state-owned banks would be offered for privatisation or wound up.

He said state-owned banks would be made to recover as many as possible of their non-performing loans, reschedule loans with sufficient collateral backing, restructure balance sheets, close down unprofitable branches and reduce bank staff.
Once that has been done, the government would start considering a portfolio clean-up for these banks, prior to eventual privatisation, he added.

The source said although Azerbaijan had not declared any policy change, the issuing of new licences for foreign banks had been frozen until further notice because of the problems facing state-owned banks.
According to central bank officials, Azerbaijan has so far issued licences to seven banks whose foreign capital amounts to more than 50 percent.
"The freeze is justifiable in view of the radical restructuring of the domestic sector, which is going through difficulties and cannot stand on its own feet at present," the source said.
"They cannot let foreign giants step in while their own banks are struggling to survive.

"The problem is that when Azerbaijan lifted the (banking) barriers, it did not calculate what the effect would be of letting in well-capitalised foreign banks right in the middle of a crisis of confidence in the domestic sector," he added.
